newsitem.title: JAPAN: Corporate share buy-backs aid rise in Japan stocks.
newsitem.headline: Corporate share buy-backs aid rise in Japan stocks.

text.p: An increasing number of Japanese firms are set to buy back their own shares for the benefit of shareholders, which in turn could boost the Tokyo stock market further, brokers said on Tuesday.
They said market participants see the trend as a sign that some companies are becoming more responsive to shareholders, and they have been bidding up those firms' shares aggressively.

The firms' attempts to boost their return to shareholders by repurchasing their shares are being looked on favourably by the market in Japan, where shareholders' rights are relatively weak and return on equity (ROE) is comparatively low.
"Companies have finally started to turn their attention to shareholders," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.

Analyst say better-than-expected profits as a result of the weak yen have encouraged some firms, particularly blue-chip exporters such as Toyota Motor Corp , to use their extra profits to reward shareholders.
The number of companies that have unveiled share repurchase schemes this calendar year already exceeds the 13 that did so last year, data from Nikko Securities Co showed.

In the first four months of 1997, 20 firms announced plans to buy back up to around 231.57 billion yen ($1.83 billion) worth of shares, compared with last year's total repurchase amount of 283.1 billion yen ($2.24 billion).

The share buy-backs were one of key factors behind the recent rally in the market's benchmark Nikkei 225 average, which rose above the key psychological level of 20,000 on Tuesday for the first time in four months.
The Nikkei jumped 666.17 points or 3.41 percent to end at 20,180.92, its second-largest point rise in 1997.

But the amount of share repurchases in Japan appears to be much smaller than that in the United States, where corporate share buy-backs in 1997 are expected to surpass 1996's record high of $176.5 billion, Japanese media reports say.
Of the buy-back schemes unveiled, Toyota's is the largest. It said late last month it will buy up to 100 billion yen ($793 million) worth of its own shares.
The planned share buy-backs, combined with recent investor buying in blue-chip issues, briefly sent Toyota's shares to a record high of 4,010 yen ($31) on Tuesday.
The recent weakening of the yen against the dollar has encouraged buying in a wide range of blue-chip issues such as Toyota, whose profits mainly come from exports.

Shares of Mitsubishi Chemical Corp a leader in the industry, also hit a high for 1997 last week on its plans to buy back up to 40 billion yen ($317 million) worth of its own stock, or up to 100 million shares.
Other companies that have announced plans include Taisei Corp a major general contractor, Citizen Watch Co Ltd and Nissin Food Products Co Ltd a major maker of instant noodles.
More companies are likely to follow suit as Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) is seeking to shorten the time needed to approve corporate share buy-backs and make the process easier.

Under current law, companies need approval from annual shareholders' meetings before implementing stock repurchase schemes, but the LDP hopes to revise the law to allow stock repurchases with only approval from the board of directors.
Helped by improving corporate profits, more companies are expected to buy back their own shares to increase their attractiveness to both domestic and foreign investors.

"More and more stocks have gained ground not only backed by the weak yen, but also by the expected improvement of their ROE," said Hiroyuki Nakai, chief investment strategist at Nikko Securities Co Ltd.
